Each packet travels on its own, so each one must say where it is going and where it fits in the order.

From 2.1. Cambridge IGCSE 0478/11, June 2025, Question 4(c)(i). A customer orders food over the internet. The order is broken into packets.

items.prompt: Which item would NOT be included in a packet’s header?
items.explain: The payload is the data itself, in the middle of the packet. The header holds the addresses and the packet number.

steps.label: Errors and Parity Checks
steps.content:
2.2 Methods of Error Detection

Errors and Parity Checks

Year 10

  • Today: why bits can change on the way, and one way to check: the parity check.
  • You already know: data is sent as bits, down a cable or through the air.
Think → Pair → ShareWhy does the receiver need to check the data, even when it was correct when it was sent?Show the answer

Something can change the bits on the way. The receiver cannot know unless it checks.

steps.label: Why Errors Happen
steps.content:
Why Errors Happen

Think → Pair → SharePredict: the letter A is sent as 01000001. The receiver gets 01000011. Is that still A? What happened?Show the worked answer

No. One bit changed from 0 to 1, so the receiver gets a different letter (C).

Something on the way changed a bit. This is called interference.

Sent

01000001

Received

01000011
  • Interference (for example electrical or magnetic) can affect data on the way.
  • A bit can be lost (data loss), an extra bit can be gained (data gain), or a bit can be changed (data change).
  • So the receiver checks the data when it arrives.

steps.label: Compare: Lost, Gained, Changed
steps.content:
Compare: Lost, Gained, Changed

Think → Pair → ShareThe same byte was sent three times. What is different about each one that arrived?Show the answer

A: only 7 bits arrived: a bit was lost.

B: 9 bits arrived: a bit was gained.

C: 8 bits, but one is different: a bit was changed.

Sent: 10110100

ArrivedBits
A1011010
B101101001
C10100100

steps.label: Exam Question: How Errors Occur
steps.content:
Exam Question: How Errors Occur

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is "the data goes wrong" not enough for the mark?Show the answer

Say HOW: interference can make a bit be lost, gained or changed.

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/12, March 2026, Question 7(c)(i). The transmitted data may contain an error.

Total: 1 mark

steps.label: Exam Question: Explain How Errors Occur
steps.content:
Exam Question: Explain How Errors Occur

Think → Pair → ShareThis question has 2 marks. What two ideas do you need?Show the answer

The cause (interference), and what it does to the bits (lost, gained or changed).

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/12, November 2025, Question 7(f)(i). The data for music and audio books needs to be checked for errors after being transmitted from the cloud.

items.prompt: Explain how errors may occur in the data during transmission. [2]
items.modelAnswer: Interference (for example electrical or magnetic) can affect the data on the way; this can cause bits to be lost (data loss), extra bits to be gained (data gain), or bits to change, for example a 0 becoming a 1 (data change).

steps.label: The Parity Check
steps.content:
The Parity Check

Think → Pair → SharePredict: even parity means the total number of 1s must be even. The data is 1011000. Should the parity bit be 0 or 1?Show the worked answer

1011000 has three 1s. Three is odd.

A parity bit of 1 makes four 1s: even. So the byte sent is 11011000.

  • Before sending, the sender and receiver agree: even or odd parity.
  • The sender adds a parity bit (here, the first bit) to make the number of 1s even, or odd.
  • The receiver counts the 1s. If the count is wrong, an error is detected.

Even parity

11011000

four 1s: even

Odd parity

01011000

three 1s: odd

steps.label: Activity 1: Parity Lab
steps.content:
Activity 1: Parity Lab

Think → Pair → ShareWhat happens to the number of 1s when interference changes ONE bit?Show the answer

It goes up or down by one, so an even count becomes odd. The receiver notices.

Set the parity bit, send the byte through interference, and check what arrives. Work through the tasks.

steps.label: Exam Question: Odd or Even?
steps.content:
Exam Question: Odd or Even?

Think → Pair → ShareThe values arrived correctly. Why does that let you work out the parity?Show the answer

Correct data still matches its parity. So the count of 1s tells you which parity was used.

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/11, June 2021, Question 8(a). A parity bit is added to each 7-bit value. All the values are transmitted and received correctly. Write odd or even for each.

Total: 4 marks

steps.label: Exam Question: Add the Parity Bit
steps.content:
Exam Question: Add the Parity Bit

Think → Pair → ShareWhen would the parity bit be 0 instead of 1?Show the answer

When the data already has the right number of 1s (here, an odd number), so nothing needs adding.

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/12, June 2026, Question 4(a). An odd parity byte check is used. Give the parity bit for each byte of data.

Total: 3 marks

steps.label: Activity 2: Be the Receiver
steps.content:
Activity 2: Be the Receiver

Think → Pair → ShareOne byte had two bits changed, but the check said OK. Why?Show the answer

Two changes keep the number of 1s even (or odd), so the count still matches.

Eight bytes arrive. Count the 1s in each one and decide what the parity check says.

steps.label: Exam Question: How Even Parity Detects an Error
steps.content:
Exam Question: How Even Parity Detects an Error

Think → Pair → ShareWhy must the answer say what the RECEIVER does?Show the answer

Detecting happens when the data arrives: the receiver counts the 1s and checks the total is still even.

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/12, June 2025, Question 3(c)(iii). An even parity check is used to detect errors in data after it has been transmitted to a printer.

items.prompt: Describe how an even parity check detects an error. [3]
items.modelAnswer: Any three: the sender and receiver agree on even parity; a parity bit is added to each byte to make the number of 1s even; the receiver counts the number of 1s in each byte; if the number of 1s is odd, an error is detected.

steps.label: Exam Question: When Parity Fails
steps.content:
Exam Question: When Parity Fails

Think → Pair → ShareWhy can a parity check never find two changed bits?Show the answer

Each change moves the count by one. Two changes cancel out, so the count is even (or odd) again.

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/11, June 2021, Question 8(b). An error may not be detected when using a parity check.

Total: 1 mark
